transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um... I guess I'm just having some issues with... work. I teach high school, and... well, we have these lesson videos. And... I just, I can't stop seeing my face on them. One side of it is... it's crooked. It looks swollen. And... I don't know, once I notice it, I just feel like the students and the parents, or the other staff... they must just be staring at it, too. Like they aren't even listening to anything I'm saying. So... yeah. That's why I came in.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly, like checking your face in the mirror, avoiding certain angles, or trying to fix how your face looks in the videos?

Um... yeah, I guess. I mean... before I post a lesson, or if I have to get on a parent conference... I do mess with the camera a lot. Just trying to find an angle that isn't so bad. And I replay the clips. A lot. Sometimes I just... I try to sit with my hand covering that side of my face. 

But mostly I just end up re-recording the whole thing. Over and over. It... it takes up a lot of time. I've been missing my prep work because of it, honestly. And... sometimes I end up late getting things ready for my classes. So... yeah. I do.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms of persistent preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance, repetitive behaviors (checking camera angles, re-recording videos), and significant impairment in functioning (missing prep work, being late) strongly point to body dysmorphic disorder. Other depressive and anxiety disorders have been ruled out based on the focus of the patient's concern and behavioral response.
